short: The last emperor of the Edo period, whose refusal to sanction foreign treaties broke the shogunate.
full:
Kōmei acceded in 1846, seven years before Commodore Perry's squadron appeared off Uraga. For two and a half centuries the throne had ratified whatever the Tokugawa decided; the shogunate's decision to consult Kyoto over the American demands handed the court a veto it had not held in living memory. Kōmei used it. He refused sanction for the 1858 commercial treaty with the United States, which was signed anyway, and the resulting cry of sonnō jōi — revere the emperor, expel the barbarians — turned Kyoto into the centre of opposition politics.

He was not, however, a revolutionary. Kōmei wanted the foreigners gone and the shogunate reformed, not abolished, and pursued a union of court and camp: his sister Kazunomiya was married to the shogun Iemochi in 1862 to seal it. He died of smallpox on 30 January 1867 at thirty-five, with rumours of poisoning that have never been substantiated. His fourteen-year-old son succeeded him days later, and the shogunate fell within the year.
